served.stem: A birch seedling, potted alone with an established fungal partner, is kept in a dark room for ten days so that it makes no new sugar. Based on the passage, the flow of carbon to its fungal partner would most likely
choices: continue unchanged, since the phosphate trade is unaffected
fall away within days, long before the ten days are up
reverse, with the fungus now supplying sugar to the seedling
rise, as the seedling leans harder on its partner for nutrients
taper off slowly over weeks as stored reserves are drawn down
served.bankWhy: Paragraph 8 gives the rule: when girdling cuts off the sugar supply, the flow to the fungi falls away within days, because the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves. A seedling making no sugar at all is the same situation, so expect the flow to drop within days.

proof.quote: show the flow falling away within days
the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves

passage.title: The Trade Beneath the Forest Floor

distractorNotes: Phosphate moving up is the fungus's side of the trade. Paragraph 8 is about the sugar moving down, and that supply depends on sugar made that week.
Nothing in the passage has a fungus feeding sugar to an ordinary green plant, and the seedling is potted alone, so there is no neighbouring tree for the fungus to draw on.
The flow in paragraph 8 is set by what the leaves make. A seedling making nothing has nothing extra to send, however much it needs its partner.
Paragraph 8 says the flow falls within days, not weeks, and that the fungi do not live on stored reserves.

answer.text: fall away within days, long before the ten days are up
answer.line: Girdling shows the flow to the fungi falls within days, because they live on sugar made that week. No new sugar, same result.

steps: Find the passage case that matches. No new sugar reaching the roots is exactly what girdling does in paragraph 8.
Read its result: the flow falls "within days", because "the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves".
Carry it over. A seedling in the dark makes no sugar, so the flow drops within days, well before day ten.

choices.text: continue unchanged, since the phosphate trade is unaffected
choices.note: Phosphate is the fungus's side of the trade. The plant pays in carbon, and that flow runs on fresh sugar, so phosphate cannot keep it going.

choices.text: fall away within days, long before the ten days are up
choices.note: Same as girdling: no new sugar, so the flow falls within days.

choices.text: reverse, with the fungus now supplying sugar to the seedling
choices.note: Fungi feed ghost pipe with carbon drawn from green trees they are also joined to. A seedling potted alone has no other host to draw from.

choices.text: rise, as the seedling leans harder on its partner for nutrients
choices.note: Needing nutrients does not make sugar to pay with. Paragraph 8 says the flow falls when new sugar stops; rise turns that around.

choices.text: taper off slowly over weeks as stored reserves are drawn down
choices.note: Paragraph 8 rules this out in so many words: the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves. Days, not weeks.
